title: An unusual case of extensive contiguous cervicothoracic spinal tuberculosis involving fourteen damaged segments: A case report
case_text:
A 28-year-old female presented to Fatmawati Hospital, Jakarta, Indonesia due to progressive tetraparesis accounting for seven months. Initially there was mild neck pain, and then she experienced numbness along with weakness of all four extremities. The symptoms were gradually worsened such that at the time of admission, she could not walk.
A series of radiographic and CT scan depicted multiple vertebral body destruction anteriorly, along with facet joint dislocation and mild retrolisthesis of C4-C5 segments (Figs. 1, 2). MR images of the cervical region was demonstrated pathologic contrast enhancement on C4 to T7 vertebrae, a total of fourteen contiguous segments, with spinal canal stenosis on the level of C4 to T4 and bilateral anterolateral paravertebral soft tissue abscess at the level of C4 to T9 (Fig. 3). Those findings were highly typical of spinal tuberculosis.
The patient was administered anti-tuberculous agents for two months before undergoing one-staged posterior-only debridement, decompression, and instrumentation. Postoperative radiographs demonstrated that the kyphosis was obviously improved (Fig. 4). After the surgery, the patient was put on a cervicothoracic brace. The patient was closely followed up, and after 12 months postoperatively, she regained neurological recovery with only mild residual neck pain. The patient demonstrated a satisfying level of functional improvement as recorded by the Neck Disability Index (NDI) and SF-36 scores of 4/100 and 94%, respectively.
Bony bridge on CT images was discovered at 18 months of follow-up, along with the normal value of erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein; it was the time we discontinued the anti-tuberculous therapy.

   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Tuberculosis
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: spinal tuberculosis
